items.title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review
paragraphs: To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.

The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.

The first exhibition begins, like so much love, with a single kiss – a gaunt couple locking lips on a 15th-century Italian vase. They don’t look too thrilled about it but, hey, that’s the reality of love. Sometimes it’s not great. The show then takes you on a salivary journey through every possible kind of kiss: political, maternal, interracial, divine, familial.

Allegories of righteousness and peace give each other an awkward peck in a William Blake watercolour, the infant Christ and St John the Baptist hold each other close in an Anthony van Dyck painting. Then a priest kisses a nun in a Benetton ad, the USSR’s President Brezhnev kisses East German leader Honecker, Cupid kisses Psyche. And that’s before you even get to the bulk of the show with its snogs by Edvard Munch, Wolfgang Tillmans and – obviously – Rodin, whose carved marble canoodle dominates the middle of the exhibition. It’s enough to give you chapped lips.

What they want you to see is the vast complexity of kissing, to understand its different histories and implications. So they show it through a postcolonial lens, a religious lens, a political lens, and so on. But kisses are not some underexplored, subconscious thing – they’re universal. We think about our kisses, we remember them, treasure them, long for them. The whole thing just feels obvious, like someone telling you the plot of a movie you’ve already seen.

There are works that deal with love more widely – including a Tracey Emin neon that says “The Heart has Its Reasons”, as if anyone on Earth needs to see another Tracey Emin neon. But they feature no actual kissing. The concept isn’t bad, and neither’s the execution, but in the end there are only so many images of people necking you can hack before you get mental jaw ache. It’s a whole exhibition of people locked in embraces, a whole show of painterly PDAs, and it wears thin.

The second exhibition, Ecstasy and the Aftermath, tackles the joy of new love, the despair of heartache, and everything in between. That’s where it really falls apart. There are some good works: a Somaya Critchlow nude, a set of deeply romantic and poetic Judy Chicago prints, a Jane Hayes Greenwood painting of leaking, breast-like plant forms, the Marina Abramović and Ulay video of him on the verge of unleashing an arrow into her heart. But the theme is so broad it sends you spinning.

There are works about motherly love, romantic love, desire, the gaze, heartache, grief. There are photos of people dancing in queer nightclubs, because community is a form of love. There’s a Paloma Proudfoot ceramic of gossiping mates, because really liking your pals is love, too. There’s so much to explore, each of those themes could have been a whole exhibition in its own right, but it’s all just been squeezed into one room.

The only way this could have worked is if they’d narrowed the focus. Or if they’d deleted all the wall texts, got rid of the faltering conceptual themes and restrictions and just whacked together a bunch of artworks about desire, adoration, romance, heartache and snogging and let you make your own way through it.
But if you want to know what love is, these two shows do actually provide a pretty good answer. Sometimes it’s beautiful, sometimes it’s joyful, but more often than not, it’s a bit of a mess.

items.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
paragraphs: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.
Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.
NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.
Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.
The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.
The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.
Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.
The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.
NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.
Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".
The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.
There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.
The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.
Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.
In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".
Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.
That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.
Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.
Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.
Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal
MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place
The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage
MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework
Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.
Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage.
The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain.
"Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained.
"Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here."
He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others".
"Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge."
His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption.
Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.
But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.
Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.
Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed.
"We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.

Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.

items.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
paragraphs: In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico, external their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.
Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.
The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.
"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."
In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.
The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.
Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.
Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers may not be able to receive emails about their trips due to the outage.
Disruptions have also been reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.
In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times, external.
The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.
Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".
Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.
In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".
In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.
Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.
Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.
European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.
In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.
"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

items.title: You know that butter bot from Rick and Morty? You can buy that now
paragraphs: Struggling to find a Christmas or Black Friday prezzie for the person who owns every novelty mug on Earth? Why not gift a palm-sized robot programmed to endure a relentless existential crisis on your desk?! Ladies and gentlemen – here is the Butter Bot.

Following a successful 2024 Kickstarter and two years of intensive engineering, creative tech studio CircuitMess is finally shipping its officially licensed Rick and Morty Butter Bot. And yes, theoretically, it will be able to pass you the butter. Better yet, it rolls around on rubber caterpillar tracks delivering deadpan commentary about the futility of its own existence. Yes please!
However, even though this grumpy little companion looks like the product of some of the best 3D printers out there, it will set you back $349. Yeah, it's for the ultra-fans only.

Inspired by a two-second gag from the intro of an Rick and Morty episode, Butter Bot started life as a cult Kickstarter project backed by 2,715 eager fans ($441,349 pledged). CircuitMess spent two years, and three electronics revisions plus custom steel moulds, turning that animated gag into a real, palm-sized AI desk robot.

And yes, of course this includes AI. Under the hood, it packs an onboard AI camera, dual microphones, edge sensors, and a remote controller featuring a live first-person video feed. Because its voice, face, and object recognition run on-device, it should recognise its owner, identify random desk clutter, read out phone notifications, tell jokes, control your TV, and – crucially – ferry sticks of butter across the table (though how the hell this is done is currently a mystery to me).

Left alone, it roams your workspace, avoids table edges, and loudly questions its own purpose. Pick it up and it panics; shake it and it disapproves; press the controller’s 'Poke' button and you’ll visibly irritate it.

Tinkerers can also snap on six modular add-ons, including an air-quality sensor, motion-sensing intruder alarm, and LED light show. O you can reprogram its open-source brain from scratch using C++ or CircuitBlocks (I'll leave that to the people in the know).
Available worldwide now at circuitmess.com for $349, it’s a wonderfully over-engineered piece of pop-culture hardware that can turn existential dread into festive cheer. If you can afford it!

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: The dark side of reselling apps: ‘If you include your pants, I’ll pay more’
paragraphs: In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged.
“So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle.
After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”.

Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function.

The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent.

In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times, over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December.

Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance.

Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.”
She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit.

“These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.”

About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.”

Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services.

Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.”

Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.”

However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18.

A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.”

An eBay spokesperson said: “We have clear policies and safeguards to protect our community, including encouraging people to keep conversations on eBay, avoid sharing personal contact details and report any suspicious or inappropriate behaviour. Where we or our customers identify policy violations, we take appropriate action.”

Depop said: “Using someone’s images without their permission is a violation of our terms of service, which explicitly prohibits users from using or sharing another user’s content without their consent, whether on Depop or elsewhere. We take the safety of our community extremely seriously and we have robust policies, controls and processes in place to protect our users.”

items.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
paragraphs: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

items.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
paragraphs: Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

items.title: Colette Kress becomes Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns
paragraphs: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang is out, and the company's chief financial officer Colette Kress is taking over as interim CEO. She'll have to guide the company through an exceptionally challenging time.

items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6038868/nx-s1-10003569" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Jensen Huang delivers a keynote at Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin on Oct. 21, 2026. Markus Schreiber/AP hide caption

A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.

Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.

He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Simone Popperl and the web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

items.title: Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture
paragraphs: French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.
Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.
“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.
“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.
At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.
It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.
“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.
“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.
It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.
Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.
In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.
It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.
Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

items.title: Farewell, Cybertruck: why the winding down of the ‘Maga hat on wheels’ is a sign of the times
paragraphs: Three days after a historic blue tsunami changed America’s political landscape, Elon Musk announced Tesla would end production of its hulking Cybertruck next year.

Was it a coincidence? Maybe. Musk said the move was “to make room for increased Cybercab production”, referring to Tesla’s Robotaxi. But the combined circumstances felt highly appropriate: it was the end of an era.

Eccentric and overhyped, the Cybertruck became a kind of automotive stand-in for Musk himself amid his political ascent. Like so many of his projects, it was massively promoted, heavily delayed, and ultimately fell short: Musk once predicted he could sell 250,000 a year but ultimately sold 70,000 in three years, losing $1.9bn in the process, according to Quartz.

The design seemed to prioritize science fiction over robust engineering: the unveiling was in November 2019, when the film Blade Runner was set, as Musk proudly pointed out – but it didn’t arrive on the roads until four years later. At that unveiling event, Musk infamously showed off the Cybertruck’s durability by having a designer throw a ball at its window, which cracked. While Musk called it apocalypse-proof, it often seemed like the opposite: Cybertrucks suffered at least five vehicle fires, four of them deadly – making them deadlier than the notorious Ford Pinto, according to an analysis. They were subject to 11 recalls amid technical issues, including a loose pedal that could get stuck and cause unintentional acceleration. They routinely got stuck in the snow.

Like its creator, the Cybertruck was highly divisive. Many observers were repulsed by its bizarre, boxy appearance and its road-hogging size (a parallel parking nightmare). “It is the ugliest vehicle I think I have ever laid eyes on,” the automotive expert Mike Caudill told Fox Business. Others, however, were deeply devoted to their Cybertrucks. “I’ve got 6,000 miles on my Cybertruck; I’ve had zero issues,” Matt Holm, president of the Tesla Owners Club of Austin, told the Houston Chronicle.

Indeed, the Cybertruck had its strong points, according to experts. “People at Tesla were rightly proud of the engineering they put into it,” said Ezra Dyer, a senior editor and columnist at Car and Driver. But “a lot of the engineering problems they solved were self-imposed” – driven by the need to incorporate Musk’s super-epic design choices.
“Why is that important to you that it be bulletproof?” Jay Leno asked Musk during a test drive. “Because it’s badass and super cool,” the CEO replied.

All this, of course, coincided with Musk’s political rise in the Trump administration. The truck, as the Guardian’s Andrew Lawrence put it, became essentially “a Maga hat on wheels”, indicating its driver’s political beliefs – or at least the politics onlookers would ascribe to them. The archetypal Cybertruck driver was a guy, “probably with some kind of goatee, likely compensating for something, so desperate for attention that he will take negative attention”, as an automotive analyst told the New York Times. Many drivers of various Tesla models rushed to distance themselves from the CEO with bumper stickers that say, “I bought this before Elon went crazy.”
The Cybertruck, meanwhile, “became this totem and symbol of Elon Musk himself”, says Dan Neil, an auto columnist for the Wall Street Journal.

While Cybertrucks took to the streets, Musk was taking a literal chainsaw to the US government as head of the department of government efficiency (Doge), which bore plenty of similarities to the truck, beginning with the empty promises. Musk said Doge could cut $2tn from the federal budget; its website now claims it has cut just $215bn. In the process, hundreds of thousands of workers left the government due to workforce reductions, early retirement and other reasons – before, in a move reminiscent of the Cybertruck’s recalls, many were rehired. And like the Cybertruck, it all came to an embarrassing end: Musk left government under a cloud as he feuded with Donald Trump over spending in his “big, beautiful bill”.

Now, when it comes to the Cybertruck, “you’ve got this expensive luxury product with a very off-putting aesthetic and all this political baggage,” Dyer says (the 2026 model runs from about $72,000 to $102,000). So it’s little surprise that sales have struggled. “It’s following the trajectory of any cult vehicle,” Dyer says. The hardcore fans line up, but once they’ve all got theirs, demand fizzles.

As it reaches the end of its short road, the Cybertruck – outwardly mighty, inwardly fragile, a poorly conceived product of an increasingly oligarchical system – feels alarmingly apt as a symbol of Trump 2.0 Phase I. Ten years from now, spotting an ageing Cybertruck on the street will serve as a reminder of the bad old days.
It will join the ranks of other vehicles symbolic of their eras – for better or for worse.

The Cybertruck is to the 2020s what the Volkswagen Transporter – AKA the VW Bus – is to the 1960s. In many ways, the two are opposites: the VW Bus calls forth images of peace and music, flower decals, and a crowd of well-meaning hippies packed inside. Sixty years after the summer of love, the Cybertruck suggests an isolated middle-aged man hiding from the apocalypse.
The vehicles do have a few things in common, however. One is drugs, but while the VW conjures cannabis, the Cybertruck is more ketamine. The other is a reputation for putting looks over safety.

A few decades later came another icon of its era – in many ways the progenitor to the Cybertruck: the Hummer H2, introduced in the early 2000s. Like the Cybertruck, the Hummer was inconveniently enormous and associated with a certain kind of aggressive masculinity.

And with its military ties and gas-guzzling reputation, it was bound up with imagery of the Iraq war. “It became a lightning rod for pro and con militarism, and so people drove them or bought them as a political statement as much as a style statement,” says Neil.

A similar perception may have plagued the Cybertruck, as Tesla showed off its ability to withstand bullets. “All of that was childish,” Neil says. “It didn’t speak with any seriousness to the mindset of people preparing to put down $80, $90,000.” The Cybertruck “represented a kind of a militarized vision of the future” to an American public tired of war.

As for Tesla’s clientele, “the wager was they were emotionally immature and it looked like a toy-slash-weapon,” Neil adds. Indeed, as the Guardian’s Arwa Mahdawi put it, the Cybertruck “looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old”. In that sense, it might best be compared to another icon of American vehicle design: the Little Tikes Cozy Coupe, the plastic red and yellow car that was for a time the bestselling vehicle in the world.
But perhaps that’s unfair. To Neil, the Cybertruck represents both a “failure of management” and “a phenomenal piece of engineering.
“Its ambition and its vision and its willingness to break the mold of convention – that I think is its legacy,” he says.

Dyer agrees. “I’m glad in a way that it exists because it’s interesting, and I’m in favor of more interesting cars. Period,” he says. In this case, however, that difference “is a towering monument to overconfidence.
“There’s never been anything like it,” Dyer adds, “and I guess there never will be again.”

items.title: Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"
paragraphs: Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.
It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.
With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.
Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.
“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.
“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”
At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.
Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.
Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.
The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.
Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.
The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.
Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.
The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.
Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.
SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.
According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.
It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.
“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.
In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.
Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

items.title: How do you redesign a cult kids’ product? I asked Yoto’s new designers
paragraphs: I’ve been obsessed with Yoto since 2019, when a friend introduced me to the tactile, lo-fi audio player for kids. My children have used it daily ever since, and it’s one of the most interesting brands out there. It arrived just as parents were looking for an alternative to endless high-stimulation screens, and it has grown from a community-led, Kickstarter-style product with its foibles into a polished, self-assured brand that still listens closely to its community.

So when I heard a new generation was on its way, I asked to speak to the design team behind the biggest shake-up of its physical design yet. It’s a fairly tricky proposition: a product used by children but invested in by parents, with a clear mission and a feature set that’s still evolving. The new players have a mischievous new look, a green dial (big news in the world of Yoto) and a few other added features. Most importantly, the design team and Yoto chose not to lean any harder on the screen’s capabilities. For families trying to rely less on screens, that’s a crucial decision.

Below is my conversation with Jack Godfrey Wood of design studio Heirloom, covering the design mission, how the players were prototyped and tested, and the challenge of designing for a product with such a clear purpose and such a vocal community.

We knew people there. One of our colleagues worked on the original Kickstarter version, the wooden cube with the two blue dials, and two of our team designed the later generations at another company. When we started Heirloom, we took on the current fourth-gen players, so our team has been involved in and out from the beginning. It made sense straight away, because we all had that Fisher-Price cassette deck as kids and this felt like this generation’s version. Once Tom and Ben showed us the community they’d built, I knew it would work.

There were technical aims and design aims. Yoto wanted more storage, more battery and more internal robustness, and they wanted the player to be splashproof. That meant a lot of work on keeping dust and liquid out. Inside, the downloads are faster, there’s more storage and the sound is better, so they’ve fixed the things I wanted fixed as a parent. Our job was to make the players fit better in kids’ hands, travel better, and be easier to hold, carry and drop without anything breaking.
Where did your design decisions come from?

Both the community and our own experience, plus writing some rules. Yoto’s core goal is “kids in control and parents in charge”. We also knew we didn’t want addictive, distracting moments. Both screens have more resolution than before, but we kept everything in pixel world, because to us that’s Yoto. It’s a fun menu, not a distracting screen. We could have added motion, like a character that waves at you if nothing happens for 15 minutes, but we felt the community would say that was wrong.
Does Yoto’s approach feel different to other consumer tech clients?

Yes. Yoto’s goal isn’t to keep eyeballs on the screen. It’s how often the player gets used and whether it adds value to a child’s and a family’s life. It’s a very clear moral code, which makes design decisions easier. A lot of the pixel work we did is artful, precise and beautiful, but we kept it happily lo-fi and didn’t turn it into another Apple product.

Yoto wanted the backup content stored in each player to be available on the player itself. That way, if you can’t find the card, your kids can still listen to what they like, and you don’t have to get your phone out at 9pm when nobody’s going to bed. The hard part was doing that without turning the screen into an iPod or an iPad.

It was our way of giving kids access to what they want without overwhelming them with 200 cards. Daily radio and podcasts have moved onto it, along with 20 favourites. It populates automatically, but parents can set up day and night versions in the app. At night, all 20 can be sleep or relaxation content. In the daytime, you can have Elton John and Harry Potter. It also means your favourites are there wherever you go, which is really good for holidays. We still love cards, though. In all our research, they’re still the main way younger kids want to use it.

For one of the players, up to 10 to 15 concepts across a few different areas. When we gave the more pebbly form to some children, it was obvious how naturally it fitted their hands and how much they wanted to hold on to it, so we presented that one with a strong recommendation. For the other, we looked at five or six directions, but Yoto wanted it to feel like a continuation of the previous products. The concept was quite singular, and we spent a lot of time on the detailing: where the dials sit, how sharp they should be, and so on.
What did you change about the dials and finish?

The dials used to be crisp. We softened them so kids can reach them from different angles, and made them slightly longer for more grip. The smart button isn’t in the middle, which most designers would do. Because it’s a kids’ product, kids can use it from the front as they hold it.
How do you work with such an opinionated community?

Because we’re external to Yoto, they do most of the community work and the feedback is funnelled to us through the Yoto team. We’re forthright about what we think is right within Yoto’s mission, and we don’t try to do everything people ask for. The challenge is that the community is always ageing up, but we also have to look after new families who’ve never used Yoto. A new user shouldn’t have to learn anything, and an existing user shouldn’t be thrown off because every feature suddenly does something else. The community’s feedback is great because it comes from hard-won experience, not assumptions.

By keeping the mischief, fun and wonder, and the underdog spirit, rather than suddenly feeling like a big corporation. My favourite bits are the hidden details. There are little faces between the dials, and the charging cable has four tiny Yoto logos, one of which is winking. No one’s going to talk about it, but one day someone will spot it and get a little flutter of appreciation.

Georgia has worked on Creative Bloq since 2018, and has been the site's Editor since 2023. With a specialism in branding and design, Georgia is also Programme Director of CB's award scheme – the Brand Impact Awards. As well as immersing herself with the industry through attending events like Adobe Max and the D&AD Awards and steering the site's content streams, Georgia has an eye on new commercial opportunities and ensuring they reflect the needs and interests of creatives.

items.title: BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda
paragraphs: Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.
The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.
“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”
If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.
The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.
“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.
Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.
“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.
Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.
“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.
Other spaces designed for refugees include an easy-build playground for children fleeing war, and wooden refugee beds designed to provide more privacy and dignity.

items.title: Why is Google cutting off Search from AI-free schools? Here are some theories
paragraphs: If schools don't want Google AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Don Ryan/AP/AP hide caption
Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.
Google is a big part of the school day for millions of students. It's not only a search engine. It's a hub for sharing documents and turning in homework.
An announcement this month makes it clear: Google wants AI to be a part of that education ecosystem.
"Parents are angry," said Jodi Carreon, a mom in Southern California. "They're very angry."

When Carreon, who also runs the advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, first read that Google was letting schools turn off AI features for students, she was excited. Her group is part of the parent-led movement demanding limits on technology in the classroom.

But even as districts including Los Angeles Unified, Seattle Public Schools and New York City Public Schools recently agreed to bans on AI in the classroom, Google did not. If schools don't want AI Overviews to appear when students use its flagship Search tool, the company said, they will lose access to Google Search altogether. Even advocates who want less tech in schools know losing the ability to "Google" something will be an issue for teachers.

In a post on X, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Google is using "its monopoly power to force AI into our public schools," and Democratic Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts wrote to Google's CEO demanding the company reverse its policy.

Tracy Pizzo worked at Google for more than a decade before leaving the company in 2022. Much of her time at the company was focused on education and ethical AI standards. Google's move this month baffled her, especially coming at a time when young people's use of AI is under such scrutiny.
She has a theory about why the tech giant is taking this stance: It could be linked to two recent court cases Google fended off in D.C.

Google was sued by big online publishers who said adding AI overview to search negatively affected their business. The publishers sued under antitrust laws, and their argument hinged on convincing the court that AI Overviews was a separate product from Google Search.

"The judge decided that Search and AI are an integrated product," Pizzo said, and subsequently dismissed the cases. "Now if Google were to provide an off switch for schools only … that's evidence that they can be separated. And that undermines the win they just had in court."

When asked for comment, Google directed NPR to its original announcement, where the company said, "Our goal is simple: provide school leaders the control and confidence to use AI products in classrooms as they see fit." The company did not respond to additional questions by NPR about any connection between its announcement and recent antitrust cases.
NPR asked antitrust experts about this theory. They weren't entirely convinced, but also didn't dismiss it altogether.
In any case, Google's AI Overviews doesn't get high marks from some watchdogs.

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that evaluates how teens interact with technology, recently gave the product an "unacceptable risk" rating. Among other things, Common Sense dinged the tool for unsafe content and citing false information.

The day after the announcement, Google came under fire for another AI product in schools. Parents in North Carolina sued the company after Google's chatbot, Gemini, helped their 13-year-old daughter plan her suicide and funeral on her school-issued Chromebook.
Even some of Google's longtime partners are surprised by the company's current position, including superintendent Hank Thiele in Illinois.
"It may have caused a lot of damage in the trust that Google has built in education," he said.

Thiele has worked with Google Classroom for almost two decades and says the company has always been a great partner. His district, made up entirely of high school students, is in the process of figuring out AI for its students. As an early adopter of tech in the classroom, he wants to be on top of it with AI.
He said he thinks the company will listen to people's feedback but they bungled the messaging.
"Google should have just plainly said, 'Our bad,'" Thiele said. "That would have been the appropriate response to a school."
The "AI or nothing" approach, as Thiele put it, did not land well.

items.title: Was the Cybertruck a flop, or a design success?
paragraphs: What went wrong for the Cybertruck? What do we know about the fire that ravaged an award-tipped new building? And why have wired headphones made a comeback? Listen to the latest episode of Dezeen Weekly now.
In this episode, Nat Barker, Jennifer Hahn and Tom Ravenscroft reflect on the news that Tesla is discontinuing its controversial Cybertruck.
After that, they discuss the developing situation regarding a Dezeen Award-shortlisted architecture project designed by Jean Nouvel that has been badly damaged in a fire.
Finally, they consider Sony’s reissue of its classic Walkman-era headphones and the wider resurgence of wired headphones.
Dezeen Weekly artwork is by Simon Volt. Editing is by Miguel Santa Clara.

Dezeen Weekly is an original Dezeen podcast in which our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the week. Listen to the latest episode using the player above or on your favourite podcast app, including Spotify and Apple Podcasts.

items.title: Nvidia chaos and why the AI industry is suddenly on the back foot
paragraphs: Until recently, the AI industry seemed unstoppable. Every week saw more powerful models, extra billions in funding, and a further spread of data centres. Anyone who complained was told: "Don't even bother. This is happening, whether you like it or not."

This month, though, things felt different. US voters delivered a blunt verdict on AI infrastructure in ballot measures, while Nvidia, the chipmaker who's played a vital role in building that infrastructure (and made RAM more expensive in the process), found itself at the centre of a spy scandal. The recent Nvidia scandal and resignation of Jensen Huang have sent things into a spiral, from a share price drop to speculation that the AI bubble has burst, even a rebranding, when we asked whether Nvidia need a new logo as well as a new CEO?

Neither story on its own spells disaster for AI. But together, they suggest something important has shifted. And that matters for the millions of creatives whose lives are being reshaped by this tech.
Most news coverage of the US midterms focused on who controls Congress. But at the same time, 40 of 41 local data centre measures decided on 3 November across 10 states favoured limiting development.

Voters approved 27 restrictive measures and rejected all 13 that would have helped projects go ahead. The results range from moratoriums and zoning limits to outright bans. And candidates who campaigned on pausing data centre construction won governor's races in Texas, Ohio and Georgia. This was not surprising, because in NBC News' exit poll, 76% of voters said they'd oppose a new data centre in their own community.

It's important to understand that this is not a partisan issue. Democrats, Republicans and Independents alike have been fighting back against the AI industry. So the timing couldn't have been worse for Nvidia.

On 6 November, The New York Times shared details of how CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of an alleged espionage operation involving a Chinese businesswoman US officials believe was working for China's Ministry of State Security. On Sunday, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with her and apologised to staff.

Huang said he had no idea she was a spy, and Beijing has dismissed the claims as groundless. Nvidia's board launched an inquiry and said it still had confidence in him. But later revelations of a second affair piled on the pressure, and Huang eventually resigned on 12 November.

Maybe I'm overreacting, but this feels like a watershed moment. Up until now, the AI industry has relied on two things: the assumption that its physical expansion was inevitable, and the aura of its leaders as visionaries above scrutiny. Now, that's changed.

That doesn't mean the AI boom is about to collapse, of course. But it does suggest the era of 'build first, ask questions later' is ending. Expect more political resistance, more regulation and more scrutiny.

For creatives, that may be a double-edged sword. On the one hand, if you're using AI tools, they're likely to go up in price. On the other hand, if you're worried about AI's impact on jobs and don't want it to scrape your work, there's a chance things will slow down now, at least a little.

Finally, it feels like a good time to remember that we actually have a voice. For years now, many of us have either kept quiet or felt like we've been shouting into the void about AI. Now that millions of voters are shouting too, the industry might actually start to pay attention.

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.
