items.title: ‘You can almost smell the sweat’: striptease artists and steel pans light up this week’s free art shows
paragraphs: A vast red concrete wall splits Maxwell Alexandre’s work in two. It’s the wall of the Flamengo sport club in the painter’s native Rio de Janeiro, a towering crimson monolith of division, literally separating us and them, rich and poor, black and white.

Alexandre joined the upmarket club in the early 2020s. He’d walked past its red walls countless times as a kid – the club is on the edge of the favela he’s from, the biggest in Brazil. What he found inside was serenity, sunbathing, prosperity, and whiteness. He’d spent his early career painting the black figures of his favela, but now he was surrounded by pasty bodies with rippling pink skin.

With success in his career, he’d bought access to this new world, and knew he couldn’t paint the same black figures he’d made his name with. So this is the result, dozens of paintings of lush tropical trees and white bodies in repose, lounging, chatting, playing by the pool within the confines of that red well, all part of his new approach to what he calls “white figuration”.

The red walls dominate the works in the first space as a figure stands on a diving board and palm fronds wave in the distance. The second room is covered floor to ceiling in paintings on brown paper of the club’s members, some shown next to figures from art history. Boys stand in the sun, men splash in the water, girls talk and women sunbathe. It’s idyllic, hazy, almost nostalgic painting.

But it’s full of emotional complexity. The work is a rejection of the expectations placed on black artists to make black work, to churn out paintings of black figures to sell to white audiences and collectors. It’s Alexandre refusing to play the game. But there’s also an introspective exploration of what happens when your life changes, when you stop being young and poor and desperate and become something different. This doesn’t feel like Alexandre mocking white flabby bodies, it feels like him trying to make sense of a divided city, an art history that doesn’t represent him, and a world that expects you to be something you no longer are. It all looks like heaven, but even heaven is a complicated place.
Carlos/Ishikawa, London, until 28 November

The exhaustion in Susan Meiselas’s photos is so palpable it’s almost draining. She spent three years in the mid-70s following a group of striptease performers as they toured the endless American sprawl, slowly gaining their trust, capturing them at their most intimate, unguarded and knackered.

She photographs them from backstage. Night after night the women dance seductively for wide-eyed, drooling, dumbstruck men – you see them gawping from between the dancers’ legs, anonymous pervs desperate for an eyeful.
And then the dancers crash from the effort of it all. They smoke distractedly, lounge on sofas or crumple into bed. This is the end result of physical labour: total collapse, utter exhaustion.
In lots of the photos dancers peek through the curtain back on to the stage, waiting their turn, watching things turn ugly for the poor performer on stage.

The more posed images don’t give the viewer much, but when Meiselas captures the dancers unaware, lost in the moment, they’re pretty special. These are stories of exploitation and entertainment, work and exhaustion, leaving behind nothing but physical, emotional depletion.
Huxley Parlour Photographs, London, until 21 November

Hyun-Sook Song says so much with so little. With just a handful of brushstrokes, the Hamburg-based Korean painter opens up a whole world: written into every mark are her memories of life in deeply rural, mid-century South Korea, her shock at the monstrous urbanity of modern Germany, her desperate need to find sanctuary in painting.

The minimalism of the whole thing is made obvious by the titles. The works are called things like 11 Brushstrokes or 6 Brushstrokes over 1 Brushstroke because that’s all they are, but they’re more complex than that implies.

She lays each canvas flat first, and paints every mark in a long, sweeping, full-body motion, physically trying to communicate her ideas into the work. The paintings are all on dark green or black backgrounds, each swooping brushstroke creating a gossamer white veil across the darkness. Cutting across almost all of them is a brown line, a stick that seems to almost lift the impossibly thin curtains. The white marks reference the raw silks collected in her youth, the brown marks nod to boundary posts that delineated her childhood landscapes. There are all these ideas of separation and division, of veils being lifted, of quiet and peace. They’re almost unbearably fragile paintings, but all the more beautiful and meditative for it.
Sprüth Magers, London, until 23 January 2027

Way before London’s Carnaby Street was one the capital’s main tourist taps, it was a proper cultural hub, a place for fashion and music to flourish. And No 50 Carnaby Street was home to six different music venues between the 1930s and 80s which helped totally change the cultural landscape of the country. Whether it was the Sunset Club in the 50s or Columbo’s in the 70s, this address is where activism met music, where jazz gave way to steel bands and sound systems, where black met white.

This tiny show in Sadie Coles’ downstairs project space by Studio/Chapple gallery celebrates 50 Carnaby Street just around the corner from the original address. The walls are painted deep brown, handmade speakers by Maya Ramnarine play out the sounds of old jazz and ska records, paintings show dancers moving in tightly crowded spaces, performers playing to packed rooms. I don’t love all the works here, but the idea is good, and the two paintings by Georgia Semple and Amida Deen are great. Semple’s is a dark, atmospheric vision of the Russ Henderson Steel Band, Britain’s first steel pan ensemble, playing to a crowd of joyful figures slowly swaying to the music. Deen’s work travels to the 1970s, with people pressing themselves together in a room of fiery red and heat-soaked orange as dub pours out of the speakers.
The show is a tiny love letter to music history, clubbing and dancing. You can almost smell the sweat.

items.title: How much art does your council own and is it locked away or on display?
paragraphs: Councils across England own hundreds of thousands artworks, but what are they doing with it all?
Fewer than one in 20 artworks owned by English councils are on public display, the BBC has found.
More than 500,000 pieces of art are held in the collections of 225 councils, but the vast majority is being kept in storage.
Local authorities remain "the biggest single constituent of public funding for arts and culture", according to the chief executive of the charity Art UK.
Yet many face a strain on storage space and resources, with a real-term fall in spending for museums leading to challenges in displaying council-owned art.
Council art collections include works by notable artists like Tracey Emin, David Hockney, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley.
Some of those collections include tens of thousands of pieces, with the largest collection of 125,000 works belonging to Waltham Forest Council.
Only a fraction of councils were able to provide the value of the collection but even individual collections had insurance values worth millions of pounds.
As of April, just 26,856 of more than half a million works were being displayed by the 225 councils who shared data with the BBC. But what options do these local authorities have?
Only one responding authority with more than 100 pieces of art - Rugby Council in Warwickshire - had them all on display.
All of its 257 artworks were exhibited together for the first time in April.
Sally Godden, manager of Rugby Art Gallery and Museum, said art had the power to connect communities.
"If things have been squirrelled away, then it's not going to do that," she said.
"It's not just a picture on the wall. It's how it connects to somebody and makes people think."
Sally Godden said the museum team aimed to ensure the council collection instilled "pride in the people of Rugby"

Godden said: "We can have the best collection in the world, but if they're not accessed, if they're not seen, if they're not enjoyed, if they don't make people think, then what's the point of them? They are so much more than an asset.

"We are very lucky to have such a great collection and continue to collect as well. By continuing to do that, we're growing stories, we're growing the diversity of the town, we're growing the views of people."
The council has backed a funding bid for the redevelopment of Rugby Art Gallery and a museum which would include a permanent space to display the council-owned collection.
Many of the council art collections are still growing and only 10 councils actively disposed of any of the art they own during the past six financial years.
Derbyshire sold 356 artworks in 2021-22, while North Lincolnshire sold 22 at auction in 2023-24.
The other eight councils said the items moved out of their collections had been donated, transferred to other museums, or disposed of.
For Derbyshire, the sale came as part of the closure of its Schools Library Service which had loaned art to schools.
When the service was closed after 72 years, the council did not have the space or staff to keep the collection.
Rugby, which is among the councils adding to their collections, recently acquired a painting selected by students and pupils living in the town
Kent did not respond to the question, but previously confirmed to the BBC it had sold 418 artworks in the 12 months to April.
At the time, councillor Paul Webb said: "The reason for selling is a practical one, with the closure of the basement store where the art works are kept.
"I am sure the works have brought a lot of joy over the years to many people, and will now continue to do so."
The council also recently sold a sculpture back to Gormley, the artist who created the Angel of the North.

The chief executive of Art UK, Andew Elis, said that if all councils were to sell off art, our lives would be stripped of "these extraordinary artworks that should be there to enrich and engage us and brighten up our lives".
Art UK has spent years photographing public art collections to create a digital record of more than one million artworks, external.
Ellis said it was "really important" to give communities access to publicly owned art.
"We own in the UK arguably the greatest public collection of art in the world," he said. "Art changes lives, it enriches lives, it enriches our sense of place.
"The beauty of bringing all this together on one platform is that you make this art available for everyone, everywhere, all the time.
"From our point of view, this is not just about getting the art up online, this is about telling the stories behind the art and giving people agency over it."
He added councils should make more use of the shared resource, especially with increased strain on finances.
Councillor Mick Barton, who chairs the Local Government Association's culture committee, said communities should be able to enjoy local art and historic exhibits.
But he said councils continued to face significant financial pressures which were leaving them with less money to provide "discretionary services, such as museums".
Once adjusted for inflation, the net spend on museums across English councils has fallen by a fifth between 2017-18 and 2025-26.
Keeping the collections in storage does not always mean there is no access to the work.
Three of the responding authorities that owned more than 100 artworks said none were on display.
One of them, Rochdale Council in Greater Manchester, is not currently displaying any of its 1,701 artworks due to the regeneration of its Touchstones museum.
Its temporary closure saw the entire collection moved into the council's stores, which had to be reorganised to accommodate the works.
Senior curator Sarah Hodgkinson said they had been "taking a bit more risk than we have in the past" by bringing items from the collections directly to the public.
That has seen a "lively" programme, including taking pieces to schools, picnics in the park or events.
It has also let them catch up on the "behind-the-scenes" tasks of looking after a collection, like the storage and preservation.
Mark Doyle said it was "fair to say that when we reopen, there will be more of the collections on display at any one time than there ever has been"
Hodgkinson said: "We've taken loads of collections out into the community as part of our collections on tour programme.
"We've been working on repacking all of our sculpture collection, making sure our documentation is being worked on."
Mark Doyle is director of arts, heritage and wellness at Your Trust, which delivers culture and leisure service on behalf of Rochdale Council.
"A lot of people don't understand what's involved in looking after a collection and making sure that it's there for future generations to be able to access and see," he said.
Doyle said they often came across the "misconception" that the museum should have all of the items on display at the same time.

"Obviously that's not possible," he said. "But also there's other stuff that people don't understand about not having things on display for too long because it begins to deteriorate or they begin to be affected by the environment."
Additional reporting by Lauren Woodhead and Jonathan Fagg.

items.title: Significant drop in levels of toxic 'forever' chemicals in England's rivers
paragraphs: Levels of the two most toxic "forever" chemicals in England's rivers have dropped by nearly a third over the last decade, according to new figures from the Environment Agency (EA).

The decline in the chemicals, PFOS and PFOA, has been put down to stricter restrictions on their use in products after increasing evidence emerged of their damaging impact on human health and the environment.
One expert studying the impact of the chemicals said it was "brilliant" to see how far the UK has come on this issue.
Thousands of other forever chemicals, known officially as PFAS, remain in use but the regulator said its report showed the need for them all to be better monitored and regulated.

PFAS were first developed in the 1930s in the US and became popular with companies making products like frying pans and firefighting foam because of their useful, oil-resistant, water-resistant and electrical properties.
They are called forever chemicals because their natural resistance means they take a very long time to break down naturally.

The earliest types of these chemicals were called PFOS and PFOA. But two decades ago researchers started to find that they were linked to tissue damage in animals and increased rates of certain serious health conditions such as testicular cancer., external
As a result, PFOS was all but banned in the UK in 2010 and PFOA in 2020.
The latest data from the regulator, published on Thursday, shows that the concentrations in English rivers of PFOS and PFOA over the last ten years have now fallen by 30% and 29% respectively.
Levels in fresh-water fish have fallen 49%.
"It's brilliant to see how far we have come in the last 10 years," said Dr David Megson, reader in environmental forensics at Manchester Metropolitan University.
There are thought to be around 15,000 other PFAS, although only around 200 are frequently used.

The EA said that despite increasing research into these compounds, "uncertainty remains regarding the toxicity of many PFAS". It said its findings "reinforces the need" for regulating all PFAS rather than one by one.

The chemicals industry has long opposed such an approach, arguing that there is currently no, or limited, evidence to suggest that other PFAS are toxic and that some have vital uses such as in life-saving medical equipment.

The regulator is now regularly testing for 60 other PFAS to build a picture of contamination across the country, and earlier this month the government announced it would begin monitoring levels in people's bodies.

The EA report acknowledged that while concentration levels have fallen, because the chemicals take so long to break down, the overall amount still in the environment is likely to have remained unchanged - they have simply been diluted and been washed into the sea.
"There is a lot to do, and this report provides an essential foundation to support investigations to make the polluters pay for any damage they have caused," said Megson.
One of the few ways to permanently destroy PFAS is by high-temperature incineration - there are just two such suitable sites in the country currently.

items.title: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
paragraphs: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

items.title: 'Summer was a wake-up call, winter could be dire' warning over food supplies
paragraphs: Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust, external, which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.
Despite 90% of the country being used for agriculture, external, only about 0.1% is currently being used for horticulture, external.
Growers at Fisher's Wern Farm, near Newtown, Powys, said this must change if the country is to survive climate change, wars and other global disruptions to the supply chain.

"We are hugely dependent and these vegetables are coming from really vulnerable parts of the world like south Europe and north Africa - the areas most prone to drought, fires, and overheating," said Fisher.

Food security has become a hot topic, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.
Fisher referenced this appeal, adding the UK "has an incredibly centralised food system with 95% of the food we eat bought from nine supermarkets".
He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.
"That is a security hazard because it's very vulnerable to cyber attacks.
"If the system goes wrong, there's no resilience in it. The food just runs out straight away."

Dibben said she believed people in the UK thought it would be able to "avoid many of the real challenges of climate breakdown" and "just be able to grow grapes and peaches" but the reality is very different.
"We're going to have to really think a lot harder about how we're producing food, even in this country," she said.
This includes looking at which vegetables work best in hotter climates.
Dibben described the past summer as the hardest she had experienced in five years of growing.
"The hours I was keeping were just insane," she said.
"I was getting out to the field at 05:00, and then working until it got just too hot to be outside, which was like 11:00 some days, maybe even earlier."
She said working in polytunnels was impossible by 09:00 due to the heat.
When it became too hot to work, she had to go indoors and "just survive until it was cool enough to go back outside at probably 17:00".
She then worked until midnight to try and get everything watered.
Dibben said she did not usually have to worry too much about not having enough water, but this year was completely different.
"Even the things that you felt like you were giving as much water as you could were still not growing as much as they should be," she added.
"We've not had the water bill yet for this summer, but I dread to think.
"We've just not had the crops to make it worth it."
She does not believe it will necessarily be as bad every year, but Dibben accepts there will be more hot summers and unpredictable weather such as flooding.
Dibben thinks there will always be a need for bigger scale farms producing wheat, barley, beef or sheep.
"But I think if there was a farm like ours every 10 miles throughout Wales, that would be a pretty great future in my eyes," she added.
The Welsh government said "significant progress" had been made on its plans to create a national food strategy to "target a more resilient, integrated and sustainable food system".
"There will also be a focus on how to grow more fruit and vegetables in Wales, and we have already begun mapping the current position of the sector with key stakeholders," said a spokesperson.

The UK government's Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said: "We recognise the hurdles that our vital fruit and vegetable growers face, which is why we are slashing planning red tape and investing £200m to help farmers trial crop boosting technology.
"The prime minister has made clear that food security is national security, and we're working across the farming sector to make supply chains more resilient."

items.title: Elliptic analytics say North Korea launders stolen Binance funds via homemade meme coins
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

North Korea is laundering cryptocurrency stolen from Binance through homemade meme coins, according to blockchain analytics firm Elliptic, describing it as a scheme designed to resemble ordinary trading and delay investigators.
The FBI on October 31 attributed the theft of than $6 billion worth of virtual assets from Binance to North Korea.
North Korea Pyongyang has denied being involved but the FBI says it has identified this specific “North Korean malicious” cyber activity as "TraderTraitor."
Binance is the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
In its November 9 analysis, Elliptic said those laundering the funds created at least six meme coins on the NEAR blockchain between November 5 and November 7.
About 117,000 NEAR — worth approximately $430,000 at the time of the analysis — passed through them.
Meme coins are tokens inspired by internet jokes, animals, or celebrities, with prices driven by online attention and speculation.
Elliptic assessed that these tokens have no apparent practical purpose other than to move funds within the laundering network.

Elliptic says the launderers created exchange pools holding their tokens and NEAR wallets that contain stolen NEAR, while other wallets in the network sold the same tokens into those pools and collected NEAR.

This replaced direct transfers between wallets with purchases and sales, potentially making recipients look like investors earning legitimate trading profits. Elliptic said network wallets conducted all sales of the six tokens. They were traded intensively soon after creation, with no trading since November 8. Each cost about $90 to create.

All transactions remain publicly recorded on the blockchain, enabling investigators to trace them. But additional steps take time to unravel, helping launderers move funds before the associated wallets are identified, and transactions can be blocked, Elliptic said.
The Binance theft occurred October 29 across 11 blockchains. Elliptic estimates losses at $6.43 billion, which is the largest cryptocurrency theft ever, according to the FBI.
Elliptic’s November 9 update put conversions into bitcoin at approximately $225 million, with $2.85 billion frozen or seized and roughly $3 billion remaining in theft-linked addresses.

items.title: Moolenaar urges next Congress to continue bipartisan China committee amid questions over its future
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

John Moolenaar, chairman of the House Select Committee on China, in a statement released November 9, urged the next Congress to renew the panel’s mandate, saying it should continue its bipartisan work on China policy when lawmakers return early next year.

Moolenaar said the select committee had brought Republicans and Democrats together over nearly four years to address what he described as serious threats posed by the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) to American interests and values.

"For nearly four years the Select Committee has brought together Republicans and Democrats to address the grave threats the Chinese Communist Party poses to U.S. interests and values," Moolenaar said. "We have worked hand-in-hand with other committees and administrations of both parties to secure vital policy changes that strengthen our nation and protect the American people."

The Michigan Republican said the committee had exposed the CCP's exploitation of the U.S. economy, American workers, and innovators. He also highlighted its bipartisan efforts to secure critical supply chains, deny Beijing access to resources and technologies needed to advance what he called its dangerous ambitions, and advocate for people fighting for freedom and dignity.

Moolenaar warned that the challenges facing the United States were becoming increasingly urgent, particularly as technological competition in artificial intelligence intensifies and China's coercive actions against U.S. allies and partners continue to escalate.
“The coming two years will be a critical period—and an opportunity to meet the moment through the Select Committee’s bipartisan mandate and work."
History of the House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party

The Select Committee on China was established in January 2023, during the 118th Congress, after Republicans gained a majority in the House of Representatives in the 2022 midterm elections.The committee was created under House Resolution 11, introduced by then-House Speaker Kevin McCarthy (R-California). The resolution passed the House on January 10, 2023, by an overwhelming bipartisan vote of 365 to 65, with 146 Democrats joining all but absent Republican members in supporting its creation.

Its creation reflected growing bipartisan concern in Washington over China's expanding economic, technological, military, and geopolitical influence, as well as the implications of the Chinese Communist Party's policies for U.S. national security and economic competitiveness.

Unlike a traditional standing committee, the Select Committee on China was established as a temporary investigative and policy-focused panel. Its mandate was to build bipartisan consensus on the challenges posed by the CCP and develop policy recommendations to counter these threats.
The 120th Congress is scheduled to convene on January 3, 2027, when newly elected lawmakers will be sworn into office.

items.title: Russian prosecutors seek 15-year prison sentence for lawyer Maria Bontsler in treason case
paragraphs: Editor's note: This story was adapted from the original VOA Russian article.
Russian Prosecutors have asked a court to sentence Kaliningrad lawyer Maria Bontsler to 15 years in prison on charges of high treason.
Bontsler is known for representing defendants in politically sensitive cases. She was detained in late May 2025 and has remained in pre-trial detention ever since.

Slovo Zashchite, translated in English as "A Word to the Defense," first reported the news, citing attorney Ilya Sidorov, who visited Bontsler in pretrial detention. Sidorov was on Bontsler's defense team until July 2026, when he was removed from the case.
Bontsler could deliver her final statement in court Wednesday before the verdict is handed down.
She was initially accused of confidential cooperation with a foreign state. Investigators say Bontsler passed information about Russian security officers to Ukraine’s SBU security service.
Authorities later reclassified the case as high treason, a charge that carries a maximum prison sentence of 20 years under Russian law.
She is currently being held in a detention center in Kaliningrad, and according to Bontsler's lawyer, her health has deteriorated in prison due to complications related to diabetes and hypertension.
Valeria Vetoshkina, a lawyer with the independent human rights group OVD-Info, told VOA that Bontsler's physical condition remains a major concern.

"Unfortunately, she is not feeling well. Everyone knows that Russian detention facilities and prisons are extremely difficult places. People are often treated poorly, and adequate medical care is frequently unavailable."
Human rights advocates have repeatedly expressed concern about Bontsler's health and the conditions of her detention as she awaits the outcome of her trial.

"If a person has chronic illnesses, they can worsen significantly in custody, and that is what happened in her case," Vetoshkina said. "She lost consciousness at one point and was not provided with proper medical assistance."
Vetoshkina also said she "would not be surprised if the sentence is close to what prosecutors are seeking."
Treason cases can carry a life sentence. But Russian law prohibits life imprisonment for women, so according to Vetoshkina, "the maximum punishment is 20 years."
The human rights lawyer also highlighted an unusually harsh approach by local security services.

"It appears that the local Federal Security Service (FSB) has taken a particular interest in this case. We see an extraordinary level of severity and a very negative attitude toward her," she said. "Given everything that has happened, I would not be surprised if the final sentence is close to the term being requested by prosecutors."
Vetoshkina also pointed out that Bontsler had frequently defended people prosecuted in cases initiated by the local FSB.

items.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
paragraphs: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

items.title: A warrior poet shares her views on the Russia-Ukraine war
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.
The war in Ukraine has been going on for well over four years, with U.S., Ukrainian, and Russian negotiators meeting this week to find a way to end the conflict.
There are currently more than two million Ukrainian veterans of the war, and the number continues to grow.
Yaryna Chornohuz knows the reality of what they are experiencing. She is a Ukrainian poet, UAV operator, and sergeant in Ukrainian Marine Corps.
VOA spoke to her during her current tour of the United States, where she is talking about the war and reading some of her poetry, much of it written about the struggles of Ukraine's military.

Chornohuz says Ukrainian soldiers are “tired and exhausted, especially those of us constantly on the front lines without any rotation." She and her husband served seven and nine years in the Ukrainian Armed Forces, respectively.
“Yet, at the same time, we all know that we have fought for and earned the right to have a voice," she says. "We live, after all, in freedom - even on the front line, even in a war of attrition.”
She also makes the case for a postwar Ukraine being led by veterans.
"They are the ones capable of building the nation-unburdened by the legacy of corruption or a focus on personal gain and instead driven by a commitment to the common good," Chornohuz tells VOA.

The poet also spoke about the current debate over female conscription. She says it's not currently being considered but, "in a war of this scale, regardless of whether or not there is a formal mobilization of women, it is essential to prepare everyone so that, if necessary, they can become soldiers."

She tells VOA she likes to joke that "if you gathered all of us - all 75,000 women serving in the Armed Forces of Ukraine - we could defend an entire small European nation. The audience at that event joked back that they would love to have an army of women like that to defend their own country."
Chornohuz also has a 12-year-old daughter. She says fighting a war and raising a child is difficult but not impossible.

"One can serve as a UAV operator and, after returning from night missions, prepare breakfast for one’s child. I did this myself while stationed near the front line, and I don’t think I’m the only one; many women manage to balance all of this."
She also shared some of her poetry, which is a way to deal with the pain of losing her fellow soldiers.
"The brightness of those eyesthe eyes of those who decided one dayto die in battleare always brighter than others’."
She is also taking time to look ahead to a Ukraine not under threat. She says that "after every war, there comes a flourishing, an era of prosperity."

"If we win this war, we will no longer be a "victim" Ukraine, nor a post-colonial state; instead, we will become a "European tiger"- a nation with immense combat experience and a battle-hardened army, capable of defending other countries in the region."

items.title: UN rapporteur tells VOA rights situation is worsening in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

A United Nations official told VOA the human rights situation in Afghanistan is getting worse, as a prestigious international affairs institute recognized Afghan women for their resistance to Taliban restrictions.

The Chatham House formally recognized the women of Afghanistan on Monday, awarding them its annual prize, in recognition of their "courage, resilience and determination in the face of systematic gender persecution."

At the same time, speaking to VOA on Tuesday, Richard Bennett, U.N. special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Afghanistan warned the human rights situation in the country “is gradually and step by step getting worse, not only for girls and women, ... but also for the whole community.”

According to a Human Rights Watch report released in August, in the last five years that the Taliban have been in power in Afghanistan, the group has imposed ‘draconian’ policies that have made Afghanistan one of the world’s “gravest human rights crises, particularly for women and girls.”

Under the Taliban in Afghanistan, women are barred from working with government and non-government organizations, attending secondary schools and universities, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
Bennett said the Taliban imposed more than 200 decrees and edicts primarily restricting human rights, including more than 100 targeting women and girls.

The U.N. special rapporteur on Afghanistan told VOA there are pressures “on freedom of expression, including for the media and public and civic space and special pressure on religious and ethnic and linguistic marginalized communities who are discriminated against, not allowed to practice their traditional religions and cultural practices.”

Bennett was appointed in 2022 to monitor the human rights situation in Afghanistan. However, he has been denied entry to Afghanistan since 2024, as a Taliban spokesperson accused him of a lack of professionalism, saying "his reports are based on prejudices and anecdotes detrimental to [the] interests of Afghanistan and the Afghan people.”
Bennett told VOA that the Taliban cannot deny their human rights violations.

“The way in which we analyze the very edicts and decrees that they have passed. They cannot deny that," he said. "Of course, we also collect evidence in other ways, visually and by talking to Afghans inside Afghanistan. There is no doubt. It is uncontestable."
He added that international pressure on the group to change its positions on human rights, particularly women’s rights, has so far failed to yield results.

“So far, the pressure is not making very much difference publicly on the surface. I think privately, underneath the surface, it is making a difference," Bennett told VOA. "And there are quite a number of Taliban who do want girls to get an education, who are even sending their own daughters to get an education. So, I think in time, this will change."
The U.N. Special Rapporteur, however, said that he remains willing to work with the Taliban to reverse restrictions on women’s rights.

“I stand ready to continue dialogue and technical assistance with the Taliban to reverse their policies, including on women's and girls' education and women's employment,” he added. “It's never too late. There is always time to change, and that change should take place."

items.title: Four grizzly bears killed in Canada after fatal attack on mother and daughter
paragraphs: "Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.

"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.

"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

items.title: UNESCO warns Afghanistan could lose a generation of professionals if ban on girls’ education continues
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

Afghanistan risks losing a generation of future teachers, healthcare professionals and other skilled workers if girls and women remain barred from secondary and higher education, a U.N. official told VOA.
“Our message is very clear: Afghanistan cannot afford to lose another generation of learners,” Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO Program Coordinator for Education in Emergencies, said in an interview.

Jaberian called for efforts to bring girls and women back to school, strengthen Afghanistan’s education system and ensure all children “can fully exercise their basic human right to quality education.”
A U.N. report, released in November, stated that the Taliban ban had excluded an estimated 2.4 million girls from secondary education, while no girls have enrolled in universities in 2026.
After seizing power in 2021, the Taliban banned girls from secondary education, barred women from attending universities in December 2022 and from studying at medical institutions in December 2024.

In addition to banning girls from secondary and university education, the Taliban also imposed repressive restrictions on women, barring them from working in government agencies and non-government organizations, going to public parks, beauty salons and gyms, and traveling long distances without a close male relative.
The group has issued more than 100 decrees that curb women’s and girls’ rights and freedoms, including their right to get an education.
Jaberian said the first priority is to immediately reopen schools for girls.
“The return of all girls and women to the education system is fundamental for us, and no alternative learning opportunity can replace their formal schooling,” she added.
Jaberian, however, said efforts should also prioritize learning opportunities for children and young people currently excluded from education, particularly girls and women.
She also said that it is important to improve the quality of education in Afghanistan.

“Strengthening the quality of education through supporting teachers and teaching and learning materials, and of course, ensuring better education data and planning, as you can see within the recently published report.”

items.title: Imprisoned Iranian human rights lawyer suffers heart attack
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Iranian human rights lawyer Amirsalar Davoudi, who was being held in solitary confinement in Isfahan prison, reportedly suffered a mild heart attack on November 8, according to Iranian human rights groups.

The Norway-based group Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), citing an unnamed source, said Davoudi was transferred to Al-Zahra Hospital in Isfahan for treatment but was discharged Monday and has since been returned to prison.

The source said Iranian authorities attributed Davoudi's deteriorating health to a change in his medication during his detention, even though Davoudi was not taking any medication at the time of his arrest.
The human rights lawyer was arrested on October 11, 2026, while attending court and defending one of his clients.

He was among the lawyers involved in the so-called “Alikhani Square” protests case. More than 50 people were arrested and put on trial for their alleged role in the January 2026 protests in Isfahan. At least 12 were sentenced to death.

Davoudi also officiated by phone the wedding ceremony of detained protesters Alireza Sepahi and Mahshad Keshani. The ceremony took place just hours before Sepahi was executed, and an audio recording of the event was later published by media outlets.
The report of Davoudi’s transfer to the hospital comes amid growing concerns about his health and personal safety while in detention.

items.title: Newly Elected US Senators Define Their Positions on China
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

From advanced semiconductor exports to Taiwan’s defense and agricultural trade, newly elected U.S. senators have outlined a range of priorities for relations with China. Their campaign platforms and legislative records offer a look at the issues they could pursue when the next Congress convenes in January.

Among the incoming Democrats, some favor tighter technology controls and stronger support for Taiwan while questioning the economic costs of tariffs. Newly elected Republicans have advocated measures addressing arms sales, supply chains and competition affecting industries in their home states.
However, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would determine U.S. policy as he sees fit, regardless of how Republicans fared in the midterm elections.

“Congress has a role to play in our foreign policy, particularly on what it funds and in its oversight function, but the No. 1 factor in determining foreign policy has always been and will remain the president,” Rubio said.

In a Nov. 5 newsletter, the New York based ChinaTalk examined the campaign platforms and records of 12 newly elected senators, highlighting their differing priorities on trade, technology and Taiwan. ChinaTalk describes itself as a hybrid think tank and media outlet focused on China and emerging technology.

Texas Democrat James Talarico advocates legislation enforcing and strengthening export controls to keep advanced super intelligence (commonly referred to artificial intelligence) chips from adversaries who could use them against the United States. He also wants data centers to pay for infrastructure they require rather than pass costs to households.

Illinois Democrat Juliana Stratton criticized Trump’s China trade tariffs in a Chicago Sun-Times candidate questionnaire, saying tariffs increase household and agricultural costs. She favors investment in infrastructure, technology and workers, while protecting intellectual property and data from Chinese cybersecurity threats and supporting Taiwan’s self-defense.

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed argues that competition with China need not lead to military conflict. His platform supports competition through research and economic strength alongside cooperation on shared interests. His SI proposals nevertheless include computing controls, customer identification requirements for computing providers and an independent safety-testing agency.
New Hampshire Democrat Chris Pappas has pursued legislation addressing Taiwan’s defense, international participation and diplomatic representation.
In 2023, he joined Republican Jim Banks in introducing the Taiwan Peace Through Strength Act, seeking faster arms sales, expanded military training and exchanges, and access to critical munitions.

Pappas also backed proposals in 2022 and 2025 to rename Taiwan’s representative office in Washington the “Taiwan Representative Office.” According to ChinaTalk, he supported Taiwan’s participation as a World Health Assembly observer and in World Health Organization technical meetings.

Kentucky Republican Andy Barr joined Democrat Ami Bera in questioning Secretary of State Marco Rubio in June about proposed Taiwan arms sales, reported delays and the administration’s commitment to longstanding Taiwan policy.

Louisiana Republican Julia Letlow helped introduce the Safer Shrimp Imports Act in 2025, seeking stronger food-safety oversight. She also joined calls for a Section 301 investigation into unfair seafood trade practices. ChinaTalk identified competition from Chinese seafood imports among her concerns.

Oklahoma Republican Kevin Hern introduced the Countering Communist China Act in 2024, addressing investment, supply chains, research, education, Taiwan and defense. His proposals include disclosure of Chinese Communist Party funding for think tanks and nonprofits, restrictions on paid lobbying, and sanctions targeting senior party officials involved in threats to Taiwan’s sovereignty.

These positions are proposals and records, not decisions by the next Congress. Senators can introduce legislation, conduct oversight and consider presidential nominations, but individual preferences do not establish party consensus.

Their congressional influence will depend on committee assignments, negotiations and legislative support. The U.S. president ultimately retains a leading role in diplomacy and policy implementation, along with the power to veto legislation.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said a Democratic-controlled Congress in January would not change the administration’s approach to foreign policy, emphasizing that the president has primary authority over its direction.

Rubio said Congress has a role in funding, appropriations and oversight, but added that “it won’t influence or change the President’s directives in terms of what he was elected to do. The president was elected to execute the foreign policy of the United States. That is a function of the executive branch.”

items.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
paragraphs: Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.
Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.
Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.
Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.
At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.
Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.
The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.
The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.

items.title: Yabba dabba doo! Could these bulging, Flintstones-style towers be the future of eco-building?
paragraphs: There’s been a geological eruption on London’s Finchley Road. Great chunks of pink basalt and igneous larvikite appear to have exploded from the railway cutting, shooting skywards to form teetering towers. Anyone trying to find Finchley Road & Frognal station need wonder no more: just look for the multistorey Stonehenge.
Countless apartment towers have sprouted above London’s stations in recent years, a result of public transport-oriented policies, but none have looked like the Flintstones were in charge.

“This is one of those stations where people are always scratching their heads trying to find it,” says architect Amin Taha, standing at the foot of his rocky megalith, an unmissable landmark next to the Overground entrance. “We’re unlikely to start building church spires or grand civic buildings with clocktowers again, so we wanted to make something people could point to and say, ‘It’s next to that building.’”

They might add that the towers, called Petra Heights, look like they’ve been assembled by a giant child, with building blocks chiselled straight from the quarry. The igneous rock that holds up these flats has been stacked with deceptive simplicity. Each slab weighs about three tonnes but they look like rustic Jenga blocks, their faces left with marks from drills and saws where they were prised from the bedrock. “Quarries normally expect architects to want everything absolutely clean cut,” says Taha. “But we just use it as it comes, saving the cost and waste of cutting. And the beauty is, you never quite know what the finished result will look like.” If only more clients were so brave.

Building a trio of six- to 10-storey towers out of solid stone may sound like an expensive proposition, but Taha says it is not only cheaper but saves a huge amount of carbon emissions compared with a concrete or steel-framed building – around 30% less in this case. If the internal frame had been made of cross-laminated timber as originally intended, instead of concrete, as built, it could have saved around 75%.

The project marks the latest step of Taha’s and engineer Steve Webb’s radical campaign to bring structural stone back into use, after more than a century of it being relegated to cladding. It follows their striking Clerkenwell Close office and residential project across town, built from similarly rugged chunks of limestone, stacked with primal relish, which was shortlisted for the Stirling prize in 2021. The duo have become evangelical about the wonders of stone, creating experimental stone beams, laminated vaults and floor slabs, using pieces of rock that quarries often treat as waste.

Webb’s firm, Webb Yates, has even developed a slender pylon prototype, exhibited at the Royal Academy, using stone’s stiffness and buckling stability to reduce the amount of steel required. It’s only a matter of time, they hope, before the industry embraces the dawn of the new stone age.

Petra Heights is their biggest proof of concept yet. It rises above the station platform like an elemental cliff, with chunks of stone bulging out at points in bouldery lumps. The three towers, which taper as they climb, are connected to a central lift and stairs, and joined by a precipitous bridge at the upper levels. Wrapped with steel mesh, the stairway is open to the elements and spills on to a lush communal roof garden, all adding to the feeling of hiking up a rocky mountain path.

The foliage will soon grow its way up the facade, as at Clerkenwell, lending it the air of an ancient ruin. In a world first, even the lift shaft is made of stone. The slabs, three metres high and 10cm thick, were shipped from Norway and assembled on site, reaching the shaft’s full height in a single day. You half expect the lift itself to be a hollowed-out boulder winched up on a rope, but even Taha’s clients have their limits.

Originally designed in 2015, the project had a bumpy ride. As is not uncommon for developments in London, the site went through three different owners before the towers were built, each time seeing the original ambition somewhat diluted as successive developers cashed in on the increased land values. The proposed mass timber frame was deemed too expensive, although Taha says the switch to concrete ended up costing much more. That change also had knock-on effects, with stone elements getting chunkier to hold up the additional weight, and braced in places by steel diagonals.

The pandemic added further setbacks. The lower floors of Sicilian basalt were already up when Covid interrupted supply, leading the remaining floors to be built with igneous grey larvikite from Norway. Both were stained with a reddish wash to match. The colour variation gives an appropriately antique feel, heightened at the base by fragments of Celtic patterns carved into the pillars, as if these venerable columns might date back much further. This archaic quality is emphasised by the names of the architects, engineers, masons and contractors being carved in a runic typeface and picked out in gold. Perhaps more architects should sign their buildings, so passersby know where to direct their praise – or ire.

“The common reaction from developers is that structural stone is too shocking,” says Taha. “They think the British population aren’t ready for it, and that people prefer brick. But if you look at the lists of the most popular towns and villages in the UK, it’s often Bath, Edinburgh, the Cotswolds. Guess what? They’re all made of stone.”

Webb is fiercely critical of the scourge of carbon-hungry bricks as the default. “Bricks are the heaviest form of decoration you can imagine,” he says. “They require a huge amount of energy to fire – often using coal – and they’re weak as shit. They put a lot of weight on the building’s frame, so the frame and the foundations have to get bigger, and they’re really inconvenient because they expand and contract, so you have to put movement joints everywhere. And they’re not holding anything up – it’s just really heavy and expensive wallpaper.”

In the last 10,000 years of building history, he argues, walls have held the floors up. But now we’ve got it back to front. “In the last 50 years or so, we’ve moved to floors holding the walls up,” he says, “which is utterly stupid.” He gestures out of the window of his office to a host of new high-rise blocks, where precast brick cladding panels are being craned on to concrete frames, each hefty piece of wall connected with steel brackets to the floor below. A stone-framed facade, however, can play the role of superstructure and cladding in one. It has a fraction of the embodied carbon, doesn’t move as much, and it’s cheaper. The slabs of Norwegian larvikite, for example, were rejects, of the kind usually used for motorway embankments.

British quarries are slowly catching up. Taha and Webb see the most potential in smaller-sized offcuts, which could be used in the same way as bricks and laid by regular bricklayers, without the need for stonemasonry expertise. They have put their ideas to the test in a remarkable “stone demonstrator house”, a temporary structure in Earl’s Court that showcases pre-tensioned stone beams and columns, stone floor slabs and a self-supporting stone brick facade.

Commissioned by the Design Museum’s Future Observatory research hub, it represents up to a 90% carbon saving compared to conventional construction. And for anyone wondering if there is enough stone to go around, Webb has a sobering fact. If all eight billion people on the planet decided to rebuild their homes in stone, the total volume required would be about the same as Ben Nevis.

Taha is busy on his next lithophilic project, a mixed-use development on the canal in Hackney using stone bricks and blocks, with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, making it “carbon negative”. Incorporating photovoltaic brise-soleil shading panels and a canal water source heat pump, he says the building will generate 135% of its energy needs. It will sell power back to the grid in the warmer months, offering a bill-free life across the year.

Webb, meanwhile, is working on a load-bearing stone option for a 200-metre tower near Liverpool Street, which he says would do away with the usual colossal concrete core and columns. Heavy, dark granite elements at the base could transition to lighter, thinner limestone pieces towards the top, expressing the structural loads on the facade, and using each kind of stone for what it does best.

“It’s a massive opportunity for architects to change it up – a reason to make a new style,” says Webb. “The first iron bridge in Telford was designed with timber-like connections, because that’s all we knew. Similarly, the first concrete buildings copied stone techniques. At the moment, we’re basically just reinterpreting concrete buildings, but using stone. We’ve shown that you can make stone trusses, stone grid-shells, really high-tech stone structures.” His eyes widen. “Imagine a future of stone electricity pylons everywhere!”

items.title: A flaccid roam through Bloomsbury’s desperately mediocre modernists: Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant review
paragraphs: The Bloomsbury Group once induced yawns as the smug epitome of a snobbish high culture but they’re now admired for their feminism and queer abandon. There’s a West End play about the loves of the Bloomsbury economist John Maynard Keynes and if you visit the National Trust’s Sissinghurst, its flowerbeds are set alight by Vita Sackville-West’s affair with Virginia Woolf.

But biography can’t set art alight, as Tate Britain’s epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings of the co-habiting Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant proves. While Keynes was quite the economist and Woolf a literary genius, I honestly can’t see enough interest in the visual art of Bloomsbury to detain anyone for long. That was true when their sex lives were spoken of in a more muted way (I read a biography of Keynes as a student and don’t remember any hanky-panky at all) and it’s true now, even as we trawl their paintings for gay and feminist meanings.

One caption for a male nude by Duncan Grant is so preoccupied with the erotic undertones, it says nothing about what is surely most interesting about the naked young man sitting on a table – that he is the same George Mallory who would vanish trying to climb Everest in 1924 and whose frozen body would be rediscovered there in 1999.

Perhaps the Himalaya is too wild to be encompassed in the sophisticated yet genteel world of Bloomsbury. Then again, so is Paris, in this exhibition. There is no French art here even though both Bell and Grant emulated French modernism, sometimes very belatedly. Grant’s portrait of Mallory, for instance, which dates from 1913, assiduously apes the style of Georges Seurat, who died in 1891.

In the early 1900s, almost every country in continental Europe was throwing up revolutionary modernist geniuses from Munch to Malevich, Schiele to Boccioni, but Britain was so visually repressed that the Bloomsbury Group seemed frightfully clever to have heard of modern art at all. It would have been more honest and interesting to show how this happened. Bell and Grant didn’t just see “post-impressionist” art, as their friend Roger Fry dubbed it, in exhibitions or magazines: they lived with it intimately. In 1918, Keynes famously hid a Cézanne still life of seven apples in a hedge near Bell and Grant’s place in the country, Charleston, because he couldn’t drive it up a muddy lane. When he got it to the house, the group all loved it.

Cézanne’s painting is a compacted philosophical masterpiece, which the Bloomsbury Group were right to admire, but it’s not here. Nor is the early cubist still life by Picasso, Pots and Lemon, that Vanessa’s art critic husband Clive Bell bought in 1911. Their inclusion would have given more context, and certainly more artistic excitement, to this show.

Instead in a section on “modernisms” (what modernisms? There was only one modernism in the early 20th century) it feels as if the wool is being pulled over our eyes. We are supposed to believe that when Grant painted Head of Eve in 1913, a simplified totemic nude like a wooden carving, he was doing something utterly original rather than catching up with Picasso’s African-inspired fetishes, or that when Bell painted her wanly cubistic Portrait of Molly MacCarthy, she was in no way influenced by having a Picasso in the house.

The problem isn’t that Bell and Grant are playing catchup with Paris. It’s that both artists appear so detached and passionless. They try on avant garde ideas but always come back to tradition. Grant’s 1920s views of the South of France have a veneer of modern style but are the kind of holiday art a Victorian painter such as Lord Leighton might have done.

Sophistication and knowledge don’t guarantee greatness, nor does having an interesting life. Tate Britain probably wouldn’t put on a show by artists who were wife and husband but Vanessa and Duncan had a unique lifelong relationship even though he was gay and she married Clive Bell with whom she had children. But the pair don’t seem to influence or rival each other in a way to make a joint show come alive: indeed they cancel each other out. The pull of queer desire that’s a recurring impulse in Grant distracts you from the quiet still observations of Bell. Here is a openly sexed portrait by Grant of his lover David Garnett, over there a painting by Bell of her sister Woolf looking melancholically introspective.

In the Britain of their day, art was barely considered a serious pursuit and, for all their knowledge of French modernism, Bell and Grant are timid about how much any of this playing with brushes matters. But then you go into a little room near the end and find something with real belief: Grant’s erotic drawings. They are totally uninhibited, explicit and beautiful. His classical yet raw depictions of men having sex are like a queer version of Picasso’s Vollard Suite and for once the influence is digested in a creative, powerful way.
It’s the only time in this show that either artist seems truly driven. The rest is the stuff of Bloomsbury costume dramas.

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
paragraphs: Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.

Shut, the new OLED MacBook Pro looks almost identical to its predecessors: a little smaller in every direction but with the same aluminium body, combination of ports and overall profile. But pick it up and the weight loss is immediately noticeable. The 14in version is 14% lighter than its predecessor at 1.38kg, which makes it only 150g heavier than the 13in MacBook Air, and the 16in version is 15% lighter at 1.82kg.

The new touchscreen is the biggest change, complete with the dynamic island around the web cam like a modern iPhone. The screen on the LCD MacBook Pro was already fantastic, but the switch to OLED has several benefits. The screen is even brighter, hitting an incredible peak of 2,000 nits for outdoor or HDR content viewing, making it one of the brightest laptop screens available.

OLED displays have individually lit pixels, which gives them dramatically better contrast with the deepest blacks and eliminates any blooming effects. That makes the new screen one of the very best on any product and a genuine joy to use to create or watch content. It is super crisp, vibrant and smooth, and makes the most of dark mode.
14in screen: 14.2in tandem OLED (3024x1986; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
16in screen: 16.3in tandem OLED (3472x2266; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 5/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC card, headphones

The OLED MacBook Pro isn’t the first laptop with a touchscreen – they’ve been common on Windows laptops since 2012 – but it is the first Mac with one. For the most part the touchscreen mirrors mouse clicks, so you can single tap on just about anything or tap and hold for right click on most things.

It also supports most of the gestures available on a trackpad, including swipes, pinch to zoom and rotate. Three-finger swipes trigger mission control so you can switch between windows, while flicking them left or right snaps them to the screen’s edge – though unsnapping them requires a mouse for some reason. Swipe in from the right side of the screen for notification centre, down from the top right for control centre and from the dynamic island for Spotlight or Siri.

The Mac is not touch-first like an iPad and there is no touchscreen keyboard. But Apple has built new touch systems that third-party app developers can use to do unique things, such as tools that fan out around your finger or scrubbing dials. Those are few and far between at the moment.

That leaves touching the screen an optional extra. Like Windows machines, it is handy to have direct interaction with something using your finger sometimes. Pinch to zoom or rotating a photo is a lot easier directly on the screen than the touchpad, as is tapping the screen to pause video. The touchscreen is also useful for performing various gestures if you use a mouse rather than a trackpad.

The OLED MacBook Pros come with the same M5 Pro or Max chips and memory choices as the regular MacBook Pros with essentially the same performance in benchmarks and during general use. They also have similar battery life, lasting for about two days of office work while mainly using the browser, writing, messaging and note-taking tools.

For more intensive workloads, such as developing and editing photos or other mid-level creative apps, the 16in version with M5 Max still managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. If pushed to the limit, the battery lasts about two hours, which is still long enough to get a solid task or two done when away from the charger.

The MacBook Pro OLED is made of 55% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available, offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED starts at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) for the 14in version or £3,399 (€3,899/$3,399/A$5,499) for the 16in version.

For comparison, the 14in M6 MacBook Pro costs £1,999, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The OLED MacBook Pro might be the first touchscreen Mac, but touch is the least interesting part about it.

The reduced weight, slimmer body and absolutely stunning new screen are meaningful upgrades that will no doubt see the MacBook Pro through another five years as one of the very best pro laptops you can get.
The light-up Apple logo on the lid is a welcome blast from the past, while the dynamic island at the top of the screen takes up less space and is more useful than the notch it replaces.

The touchscreen is best thought of a value-added extra that is useful on occasion or for certain types of tasks. This isn’t a touch-first laptop, it’s more like one that just happens to have a touchscreen similar to many of the best Windows rivals, which is just fine.

I still wish the dynamic island contained Face ID like it does on an iPhone. The Touch ID fingerprint scanner is fine, but face recognition on a laptop is better. And no matter how you slice it, any of the new MacBook Pros cost a lot of money, part of which can be blamed on RAMageddon.

As crazy as it might sound, if you’re currently hoping to replace an older machine with a new high-end M5 Pro or Max Apple laptop, the extra £400 or equivalent for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is worth it over the regular LCD MacBook Pro.

Pros: stunning OLED touchscreen, dynamic island with great Centre Stage camera, thinner and lighter, choice of extremely potent M5 Pro or Max chips, long battery life, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, brilliant speakers, Touch ID, first-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: extremely expensive, no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, touchscreen only occasionally useful.

items.title: Iraq say it has made progress in talks with armed groups
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
The Iraqi government has made significant progress in talks with armed militia groups and that five of them had agreed to place their weapons under state control, a government spokesman told VOA.
“The government has completed the requirements and the details of negotiations” with five, armed groups, spokesman Haydar al-Aboudi told VOA Kurdish reporter Diyar Jamal in an interview in Baghdad.
Aboudi also said talks continue with two other groups, and that the hope is that those negotiations will be concluded successfully by June 2027.

Aboudi did not name the groups or explain and questions about the negotiations have yet to be announced, and it’s unclear if the militias have agreed to surrender their weapons or join Iraq’s official security forces.
The issue of armed groups operating outside government control has been a longstanding concern. Some of the country’s most powerful armed factions have close ties to Iran.
Washington has repeatedly called on Baghdad to bring all weapons under government control and prevent armed groups from acting independently.
Aboudi said the government had taken steps to address the issue since Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi took office in May 2026.
He said June 2027 was the deadline set by the government to complete the process.

U.S. envoy Tom Barrack on Sunday praised Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi for taking action against Iran-backed militias. He singled out the government's decision to cancel some contracts at Mosul International Airport over alleged links to armed groups. The contracts cover airport counters, parking facilities and taxi services, and Zaidi suggested they be awarded to international companies. Barrack said al-Zaidi was sending a clear message that “militia influence has no place in Iraq’s institutions,” calling the move “sovereignty in action.”
Aboudi described Iraq’s relations with Washington as moving toward greater economic cooperation based on shared interests and mutual respect.
The United States and Iraq agreed on a phased transition of the coalition’s military mission, with Iraqi forces taking greater responsibility for the country’s security.
